title: You were strangers
hook: love the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt (Deuteronomy 10:19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leviticus nineteen. Your line was love has hands. Did you do your neighborly thing? Today, the Torah widens the circle past the neighbor, to the one who just arrived. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

The first week in a new place has its own feel. Nobody tells you which door people actually use, how the bus takes payment, who to ask about the trash. You smile too much, or not enough. The Torah returns to that position more than once, the newcomer's, and asks its readers to remember standing in it. This first week of the love block ends right there, with the stranger.
screen: `A FIRST WEEK SOMEWHERE NEW.` → `THE NEWCOMER'S PLACE.`

segments.voice: First, love the stranger. In Deuteronomy, Moses describes God as the one who loves the stranger, giving him food and clothing, and then says: "Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason isn't an argument. It's a memory. Second, as thyself, again. Yesterday's chapter, Leviticus nineteen, says it too. The stranger who lives with you shall be as one born among you, "and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The love owed to the neighbor is stretched, on purpose, to the outsider. Third, the heart of a stranger. Exodus puts it plainly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Empathy, in this text, isn't imagination. It's history carried in the body. Fourth, the week in one line. This week climbed Diotima's ladder, met Aristophanes' halves, sorted Aristotle's friends, found another self, sat with Montaigne's La Boétie, and read Leviticus. It began with one beautiful face and one chosen friend, and came round to the neighbor. The stranger widens the circle again: someone not chosen, not yet known, whom the Torah asks its readers to welcome anyway.
screen: `LOVE THE STRANGER.` · `AS THYSELF, AGAIN.` · `THE HEART OF A STRANGER.` · `THE WEEK IN ONE LINE.` · then, large: `YOU WERE STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let a newcomer come to mind: someone new at work, in your building, at your table, in your town. Breathe in, and remember a time you were the new one: what you didn't know, who helped, who didn't. Breathe out, and let that memory turn toward them. Then find one thing you wish someone had told you when you were new, the door people actually use, the person to ask, and plan to tell it to them. The bell holds the time.
Moses. In Deuteronomy, he gives the reason for loving the stranger: not an argument, but a memory of being one. Today's word.
Your line: history carried in the body. Today, welcome one newcomer by telling them the one thing you wish someone had told you. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition cites the Torah's command to love the stranger, remembering slavery in Egypt, in teaching about welcoming guests and newcomers, and the memory of Egypt is retold each year at the Passover seder.
